name: Quercitrin

card.summary: A plant flavonoid glycoside sometimes floated for hair, with antioxidant lab data but no hair studies in people.

quick.overview:
Quercitrin is a flavonoid found in buckwheat, oak and some herbal extracts. It is discussed as a possible hair-supportive plant compound because of its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in lab studies.

No published human trial has tested it for hair growth, so its appearance benefit is unproven.
quick.mechanism: In animal and cell studies it is broken down to quercetin and dampens inflammatory signalling such as NF-kappaB and iNOS. None of this has been shown in hair follicles.
quick.risks: Safety for hair use has not been studied. Dietary exposure through plant foods is common; concentrated topical or supplement use has no published hair-related safety data.

lead: Quercitrin (quercetin 3-rhamnoside, also called thujin) is a flavonoid glycoside in which the flavonol quercetin is bound to the sugar rhamnose [1]. It occurs in plants such as Tartary buckwheat and several oak species, and is a component of the dye quercitron [1][2].

In hair-care discussion it is floated as a plant flavonoid that might support the scalp through antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, the same properties for which quercetin and related flavonoids are popular in supplement circles. T Nation forum posts describe quercetin as the backbone for several other flavonoids including rutin, quercitrin and hesperidin [8]. The wiki lists it because it sits in this group of plant compounds people look at when researching hair health.

Published research on quercitrin itself concerns antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in cells and animal models, mainly in the gut, immune cells, heart and brain [3][4][9][10]. No published human study has tested quercitrin for hair growth or hair loss.
infobox: Tartary buckwheat, oak species, St John's wort extracts [1][2]

paras: Quercitrin has a molar mass of about 448 g/mol. The enzyme quercitrinase hydrolyses it to L-rhamnose and quercetin [1]. Tartary buckwheat herb contains quercitrin at roughly 0.01 to 0.05 percent of dry weight, alongside much larger amounts of rutin [2]. Quercitrin is also one of the flavonoids reported in extracts of Hypericum perforatum [5].
Human gut bacteria can cleave flavonoid glycosides such as quercitrin to release the aglycone quercetin, a step reported in early work on intestinal Bacteroides strains [6].

Wikipedia also lists white oak (Quercus alba), English oak (Quercus robur), Nymphaea odorata and Taxillus kaempferi among natural sources, and says it has been investigated as a potential dietary supplement [1]. The Austrian chemist Heinrich Hlasiwetz (1825 to 1875) is remembered for his chemical analysis of quercitrin [1].

In a mouse model of intestinal inflammation, researchers found that the anti-inflammatory effect of quercitrin involved release of quercetin and down-regulation of the NF-kappaB pathway [3]. A related study associated quercitrin's effect with reduced iNOS expression [7]. In a cell-culture study, quercetin and quercitrin both reduced inflammatory and oxidative markers in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophage-like cells [4].

In the mouse model, quercetin itself had not shown benefit in vivo, whereas its glycosides, including quercitrin, did, which the authors attributed to quercetin release in the gut [3]. A separate study in macrophages reported that quercetin, but not rutin or quercitrin, prevented hydrogen peroxide-induced apoptosis through antioxidant activity and heme oxygenase 1 expression [11]. A study of human volunteers reported that flavonoid glucosides are hydrolysed in the oral cavity [12]. A flavonoid-rich Hypericum perforatum extract that includes quercitrin showed antioxidant activity in vitro [5], and flavonoids from the same plant were reported to show antidepressant-like activity in a forced swimming test in animals [13].

These findings are not hair-specific. Inflammation and oxidative stress are themes in some hair-loss research, which is the reason given for interest in flavonoids generally, but no source reviewed here links quercitrin to hair follicles.

More recent laboratory and animal papers describe quercitrin improving cardiac remodeling after myocardial infarction in a mouse model by regulating macrophage polarization [9], reducing microglia-driven inflammation and cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease mice [10], and inhibiting the type III secretion system of Salmonella Typhimurium [14]. An editorial discussed its potential role in preventing prostate and bladder cancer [15], and a cell study reported that quercitrin restrained growth and invasion of lung adenocarcinoma cells [16]. These studies do not concern hair.

No studies found. Related laboratory and animal work on quercitrin and quercetin addresses inflammation and antioxidant activity, not hair [3][4][7]. A randomized trial from 1998 examined flavonoids and vitamin C on oxidative DNA damage in human lymphocytes, a study of dietary flavonoids as a class rather than of quercitrin for hair [17].

timeline.event: Study reports hydrolysis of dietary flavonoid glycosides such as quercitrin by human intestinal Bacteroides [6].
Mouse study shows quercitrin's intestinal anti-inflammatory effect involves release of quercetin and NF-kappaB down-regulation [3].

angle.text: Proponents of plant flavonoids point to antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity as a route to a healthier scalp environment. That chain is a hypothesis: the studies of quercitrin address inflammation in non-hair tissues, and no hair-specific results are published.
